# Margaret's Testimony

Margaret Chen had spent thirty-four years as a forensic analyst, methodical and precise, building a reputation for meticulous case work that had helped secure convictions in three dozen homicides. She was sixty-eight when the assault happened—a Tuesday evening in the parking garage beneath the courthouse, after she had stayed late to finalize testimony for the following morning. A man she did not know approached from behind the concrete pillar near her car. She remembered his hands first: large, scarred across the knuckles, one of them grabbing her wrist with such force that she heard the tendons creak. She fought. She was strong for her age, but he was stronger, and what he did to her in those twelve minutes left her with a fractured collarbone, lacerations across her shoulders, and a constellation of injuries that the hospital documented with clinical precision—the same precision Margaret herself had once applied to crime scenes. Now, three years later, she carried those hands with her everywhere.

The first months after the assault, Margaret had tried to return to work. She sat at her laboratory bench as she always had, examining trace evidence under the microscope, but something had fractured in her that no X-ray could detect. When colleagues mentioned upcoming cases—next month's trial, plans for the department's autumn conference—the words landed like a threat. Talking about the future, any future, sent her into a state of dread so acute that she would excuse herself to the bathroom. She could not say why, only that the thought of months or years stretching ahead felt impossible, as though she were being asked to walk toward a cliff she could not see. Within six months, she had taken early retirement.

At home, Margaret had come to arrange her life around a single principle: she must always see what was coming. She moved the dining room chair so her back pressed against the wall at every meal. When she and her husband, Robert, sat in the living room, she positioned herself where she could monitor the doorways. Robert had stopped asking why. He had also stopped asking her to join him on their evening walks, the ritual they had maintained for forty years, because Margaret no longer exercised. The thought of being outside, vulnerable, with her back to the world, made her chest tighten. She had not walked more than the distance from her car to a store entrance in nearly three years. Her weight had dropped steadily. Food had become something she could control—the only thing left that felt like control—and she had learned to suppress hunger as a kind of discipline, a way of proving to herself that her body still obeyed her will. Some days she ate a yogurt and an apple. Robert worried. He left prepared meals in the refrigerator. She threw most of them away.

The memories themselves had become a landscape she could no longer fully enter. When she tried to recall what happened, the rage would rise first—a fury so consuming and directionless that she would grip the edge of whatever surface was nearest to her, her jaw locked. But the rage was also a wall. Before she could move past it, before she could see the full shape of what had occurred, she would feel herself pushing the memory away, as though her mind were slamming a door. Other times, usually late at night, she could see fragments with an eerie clarity—his face, the texture of the concrete under her palms—but the emotions would be absent, as if she were watching a film about someone else's catastrophe. She was certain that if she allowed herself to think about the event fully, to hold all of it at once, she would shatter. That fear was the reason she had not told anyone except Robert, and even to him, only the bare facts.

Margaret had come to believe that happiness was something that had belonged to another version of herself, one who no longer existed. The woman who had loved her work, who had laughed at Robert's terrible jokes, who had felt capable and whole—that Margaret was gone. What remained was someone inadequate, broken, a shell that looked like a person. She was seventy-one now, and she could not imagine feeling otherwise. It was her daughter's insistence that finally brought her to the therapist's office, after Margaret had missed her granddaughter's birthday party and could not explain why. Margaret sat in the waiting room with her back to the wall, as always, and waited to be called.
